newsitem.title: UK: Study finds more evidence of genetic cause of MS.
newsitem.headline: Study finds more evidence of genetic cause of MS.

text.p: British researchers said on Friday they had found more evidence that people with the muscle-wasting disease multiple sclerosis (MS) had a higher than average chance of passing it onto their children.

"In general the current theory of multiple sclerosis is that there is a genetic component, so people are born at risk...but that genetic susceptibility is triggered by outside factors," said Jeremy Chataway, a neurologist at Addenbrooke's Hospital in Cambridge who worked on a study of MS.
Chataway said the study, published in the medical journal Lancet, strengthened the argument for studying the role of genes in passing on the disease.
The study of 45 couples who both had MS showed that five, or six percent, of their children also had the disease. Another five had signs of the disease but had not yet developed full symptoms.
That made for a one-in-17 incidence in children of couples with MS, compared to a one-in-200 risk in the general population.
"That leads toward the genetic," Chataway said in a telephone interview. "It's really just another piece in the puzzle pointing to the importance of the genetic contribution."
Chataway said theories abounded about what caused MS to develop in genetically susceptible people, from a virus to a vitamin deficiency to trauma in pregnancy.
He said there could be four or five genes that put people at risk and researchers were looking for these.

The report said 33 of the couples in the study had met and married before they knew they had MS -- which can develop from childhood into adulthood. Chataway said the report had implications for couples who meet at MS clinics.
